title: Archimedes' Two Methods: Conic Sections and the Limits of Ancient Analysis
content: This file addresses three conic sections: the circle (Archimedes' main result, ~250 BCE), the ellipse (via scaling from the circle), and the parabola (Archimedes' *Quadrature of the Parabola*, ~250 BCE). All three have elementary closed-form areas discoverable by exhaustion. The hyperbola's area ∫₁ᵗ (1/x)dx = ln(t) requires the logarithm — a transcendental function beyond exhaustion methods. The file formalizes two key contributions: (1) the algebraic structure of Archimedes' geometric series 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + ... = 4/3 (the parabola result, the oldest infinite series in history); (2) the general exponential convergence principle C·rⁿ → 0 for 0 < r < 1. The noncomputable section is required because Real.pi appears in the ellipse formulas and is not computable in Lean.
mathContext: Three bounded conics: circle (area $\pi r^2$), ellipse (area $\pi ab$), parabolic segment (area $\frac{4}{3}T$). All three Archimedes computed via exhaustion. Fourth conic: hyperbola (area $\ln t$) — transcendental, beyond elementary methods. Key contrast: parabola exhaustion converges geometrically (ratio $1/4$); circle exhaustion converges polynomially ($O(1/n^2)$).

title: Ellipse Area Theorems: Algebraic Placeholders for Scaling
content: Four theorems formalize the circle and ellipse area relationships. `circle_area` is a tautology ($\pi r^2 = \pi r^2$ by `rfl`). `ellipse_area_from_circle` proves $ab\pi = \pi ab$ by `ring`. `ellipse_area` proves $\pi ab \geq 0$ by `positivity`. `circle_is_ellipse` proves $\pi r r = \pi r^2$ by `ring`. These are algebraic tautologies, not genuine geometric proofs. The actual mathematical content — that area scales by the Jacobian determinant $ab$ under the linear map $(x,y) \mapsto (ax, by)$ — is stated in the docstrings but not formalized. A complete proof would use Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.Measure.map_linear` or the change-of-variables formula. This gap is explicitly acknowledged.
mathContext: The affine map $(u, v) \mapsto (au, bv)$ has $|\det| = ab$, so for any measurable $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$: $\lambda(T(S)) = ab \cdot \lambda(S)$. Taking $S$ = unit disk gives $\text{Area}(\text{ellipse}) = ab \cdot \pi r^2|_{r=1} = \pi ab$. In Lean, this requires `MeasureTheory.Measure.map_linear` or Cavalieri's principle. The current `ring`/`rfl` proofs only verify the algebraic identity of the final formulas.

title: Archimedes' Parabolic Exhaustion and Geometric Series Formula
content: The Part 2 section header and docstring describe Archimedes' method for the parabola (~250 BCE): inscribe a triangle $T_0$ with area $T$; in the two remaining segments, inscribe triangles each with area $T/4$; continue indefinitely, obtaining the geometric series $T(1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + \cdots) = T \cdot 4/3$. `geom_sum_formula` formalizes the finite partial sum identity $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} r^k = (1 - r^n)/(1-r)$ for $r \neq 1$ by induction: the base case ($n=0$) gives empty sum $=0$ via `simp`; the inductive step rewrites using `Finset.sum_range_succ` then closes by `field_simp; ring`. This is Euclid *Elements* IX.35 for general real $r$.
mathContext: The geometric series $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} r^k = (1-r^n)/(1-r)$ is known since antiquity. Archimedes applied it with $r=1/4$ to compute the parabolic segment area. The Lean proof follows the standard induction: $S_{n+1} = S_n + r^n = (1-r^n)/(1-r) + r^n = (1-r^{n+1})/(1-r)$. Mathlib also provides `Finset.geom_sum_eq` for this identity.

title: Archimedes' Series at r=1/4: Partial Sums and Parabolic Area
content: `archimedes_partial_sum` specializes `geom_sum_formula` to $r=1/4$: $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (1/4)^k = (4/3)(1 - (1/4)^n)$. `archimedes_remainder` derives the error $4/3 - S_n = (4/3)(1/4)^n$ by `ring`. Then the parabolic section: `parabolic_segment_area` gives the $n$-step approximation $T \cdot S_n$; `parabolic_area_error` states the error is $T \cdot (4/3)(1/4)^n$ (by `ring` from `archimedes_remainder`); `parabolic_area_error_pos` proves this error is strictly positive via `positivity` (since $T > 0$ and $(1/4)^n > 0$). These three theorems mirror the circle convergence structure from the parent file (OQ03-OQ01).
mathContext: The 4/3 appears because $1/(1-1/4) = 4/3$. For $n=4$: $(4/3)(1/4)^4 = 4/(3 \cdot 256) \approx 0.0052$, so the 4-step approximation is $99.5\%$ accurate. Comparison: the circle inscribed hexagon ($n=6$) has error $\approx 4.5\%$. This exponential convergence ($r=1/4$) vs. polynomial convergence ($O(1/n^2)$ for circles) shows the parabola method is asymptotically more efficient.

title: General Exhaustion Principle: Error Positivity and Vanishing
content: Part 3 abstracts the exhaustion principle to any geometric sequence error $C \cdot r^n$ with $0 < r < 1$. `exhaustion_convergence` proves $C \cdot r^n > 0$ by `positivity` — the approximation always falls short (exhaustion from below). `exhaustion_error_small` is the substantive theorem: for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ with $C \cdot r^N < \varepsilon$. The proof unpacks `tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one` (which gives $r^n \to 0$) via `Filter.Tendsto` + `Metric.tendsto_atTop` to extract $N$ with $|r^N| < \varepsilon/C$, then multiplies by $C$ via `mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left`. This is the $\varepsilon$-$N$ formalization of geometric convergence.
mathContext: The theorem `exhaustion_error_small` formalizes: $\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N: C \cdot r^N < \varepsilon$. The proof pipeline `tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one → Filter.Tendsto → Metric.tendsto_atTop → ∃ N` is a standard Mathlib pattern for extracting quantitative convergence witnesses from abstract limit statements. The `positivity` tactic for `exhaustion_convergence` handles $C > 0, r > 0 \Rightarrow C \cdot r^n > 0$ automatically via `pow_pos` and `mul_pos`.

title: Summary: Method of Exhaustion for Three Conic Sections
content: The closing summary (lines 166-190) draws together the three results. (1) Ellipses: area $= \pi ab$ via affine scaling with Jacobian $ab$ (algebraically verified but measure-theoretically incomplete). (2) Parabolic segments: area $= (4/3)T$ via Archimedes' geometric series $1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + \cdots = 4/3$ (the oldest infinite series result in history, formalized by `geom_sum_formula` + `archimedes_partial_sum`). (3) General principle: exhaustion with geometric convergence $C \cdot r^n \to 0$ covers all three cases — circles ($r \approx O(1/n^2)$ polynomially), ellipses (same via scaling), and parabolas ($r = 1/4$ geometrically). The summary explicitly answers the open question: YES, the method of exhaustion generalizes to ellipses and parabolas.
mathContext: The answer 'YES' to the OQ corresponds to the classical theorem: every area computable by a convergent exhaustion method has a Lean formalization via `exhaustion_error_small`. The three methods differ in convergence rate: parabola ($r=1/4$, exponential), circle/ellipse ($1/n^2$, polynomial). The summary comment serves as mathematical context for the gallery, explaining the broader significance of `exhaustion_error_small` as the abstract principle underlying all three exhaustion arguments.
